channel.title: Impregnating Ultrasound (Tale)
channel.description: Posts in the discussion thread "Impregnating Ultrasound (Tale)" - She loves him like her own, she'll have him as her own. After all, how is a sterile woman to have a baby?

item.title: Re: Impregnating Ultrasound (Tale)
item.content:encoded:
Here's a tiny smidgen of crit:

[+] Open
[-] Close

The night breeze was cool and dry, unbelievably rare for Florida, even in Winter.

Winter is not a proper noun and as such, shouldn't be capitalized.

She sat back in her car for a moment longer, just one moment longer

This line is fine, but located a paragraph down from that quote is the line, "thinking about his blue, blue eyes" which might come off as repetitive.

Hers were brown. She turned off her car, stepped out and close the door behind her.

Should be "closed." Imo, there's too many "hers" here.

Damned global warming and such.

I personally don't really like the "and such" tacked on at the end.

She walked over to her front door and went through her keys, searching for the one to her house.

Same thing as earlier, so many "hers."

the door clicked open from the other side and slid open

I've never heard of a sliding front door, but that might just be me. Slightly more important crit goes to the use of "open" twice.

she stepped into the house and locked the front door.

You've already stated that this is the front door, no need to do it again.

She rested him on her lap, with him leaning deeply into her belly.

I'd change this around to use "leaned" rather than "leaning" to keep with the past tense, something like, "She rested him on her lap while he leaned deeply into her belly."

she dug her fingernails into his scalp and felt him shiver under her touch. As he always did, every single night.

I'd make this all one sentence, I think you'd just need to remove the period and that'd be it.

"Did you shower yet?" Lisa asked her.

Her kid suddenly switches gender.

He nestled his hair deeply into Lisa's bosom, quickly feeling a second pair of arms wrap around him; the arms of unconsciousness.

I'd change it to "bosom and quickly felt" to keep with the past tense. "The arms of unconsciousness" make it sound like Lisa fell asleep, but it was James that fell asleep? It could also be interpreted that the arms of unconsciousness make people fall asleep, either way, I think it's too vague.

His breath came out tiny, mousy snores.

add "in" after "out."

Lisa felt a tiny smidgen of drool drop on her shoulder.

There's nothing inherently wrong here, but consider removing "tiny" because "smidgen" is already a small amount of something, so you have a "tiny small amount of something."

peered deeply at his peaceful, pale, pudgy face.

Personal opinion, I don't particularly like the use of three adjectives here, especially the fact that they all start with a "p."

She tapped them against the table

I could be wrong here, but I think it's supposed to say "taped" even if it is or isn't it's of a weird thing to do, tapping paper against a table or taping paper against a table just doesn't seem like something people do?

Just then,

You have used this a couple times, consider switching one of them out to avoid repetition.

SIGNATURE: Lisa Goldsman

If you're interested I could show you how to make that into a written signature on the page rather than it just being typed out in the generic font.

Test results from a few years back. Test results for severe chlamydia.

This is the third time you use this kind of purposeful repetition (the first two being "just a moment longer," and "blue, blue eyes") I'd consider changing some of them out to avoid repetition in the repetition.

She allowed herself a slight frown, deadened and dulled by time, folded up the papers and put them back in the drawers.

This is clunky if you say it aloud? It just doesn't feel right for the pacing of a sentence. And why are the papers for her test results stored in multiple different drawers?

And then she crawled into bed and went to sleep.

I think this would work better with descriptors rather than "and then" eg: "Weathered and weary, she crawled into bed and went to sleep."

Lisa pat James on the head and opened the front door

She's multitasking! Patting her kid on the head and opening the door at the same time!

She stepped aside and ushered Sammy inside.

I don't particular like the similarity of "inside" and "aside" being used here, I'd replace "inside" with "into the house" or some such to avoid the repetition.

she picked up the three year old, spun the squealing, smiling three year old

No need to say he's three years old twice.

Lisa waved in response.

This, to me, sounds like Lisa put on her shoes and stood in the hall a couple feet from James and just stood there and waved, she didn't even leave, just stood there and waved for no discernible amount of time. I'd rephrase this to something like, "Lisa waved back to him while strolling out the door."

She did not stop to humor him; she said nothing and walked away.

This is basically the same sentence written twice.

rather concerning for a woman at age twenty-seven

I'm not sure how I feel about the phrasing of "age twenty-seven" but this is good characterization, her age doesn't seem overly forced in here, it's good.

frantically looked around at her colleagues and looked back to the ultrasound room.

More multitasking, she's looking at her colleagues and looking back to the room at the same time, I don't even think that's possible!

looked back to the ultrasound room. She didn't know why she was doing this, but she didn't care.

The second sentence here I believe is supposed to refer to her going to the ultrasound room, but it's stated before she actually does anything and comes off as referring to her looking toward the room.

This time, not with a stiff lip and white knuckled grip; this time, with wide eyes and a confused gaze.

This is that same purposeful repetition, you use it too much!

What the hell is going on…?

I'm not really a fan of the "…?" but that's really just personal preference.

Quick note: I think the anomalous stuff was introduced very smoothly and in a timely manner where her struggles were sufficiently set up and it is still unclear how it'll be of benefit to her, I really like how you managed that.

Until the third trimester.

a few lines after this, you use "until now" and it's a little tiny bit repetitive.

Another quick note: holy fucking shit that was absolutely terrifyingly brilliant and horrifying, I think you leave just enough details vague that the reader fills in the blanks and it is fucking well done. The only criticism that I have on that part is that the falling action feels like it plummets and then ends a bit quick.

And ran. And drove

These two lines together like that sound a bit off, perhaps she runs all the way home and has to go back for her car later? I just really don't like the "and drove" bit.

Nobody could.

I really like that line, it adds a lot for being so short.

St. Mary's Hospital.

If that's the one in PA, I've been there (toddler-me smashed his dumbass head into a wall.)

Lisa caressed his brown little curls and little scratched a nail down his forehead and bridge of his nose, earning a little giggle from him.

Little, little, little. Also, I'm not sure what "little scratched a nail down his forehead" means? I think it's a mistake?

his pudgy little smile

This is the second time you call him "pudgy."

closely examining every wrinkle on her face.

Correct me if I am wrong, but earlier she said she didn't care about her wrinkles and this moment shows her becoming more concerned about such things and it is great characterization, which is something that is exuded by this tale.

Her gaze slowly shifted to her belly

The paragraph that starts with this sentence is a great paragraph, my only issue with it is that you use the word "belly" three times.

She gazed at his curly sandy hair

This is the second time you call his hair "curly sandy." I had some previous crit on the first use of it because I didn't realize that sandy was the color of his hair and I thought that his hair actually had sand in it. Consider clearing that up because I don't think "sandy" is generally immediately associated with the color of sand and rather something having sand in it.

This was what she wanted, even if James didn't. But he'd make her want it.

I believe these are contradictory statements, James doesn't want it, James will make her want it.

I was about to critique the word "quiet" because I thought you spelled it wrong, but it was just a bit of jamais vu and I'm an idiot.

"Okay!" James whispered loudly.

This is a nice touch.

The next three trimesters would be lonely, but oh, so worth it.

I'd remove the comma after "oh."

The first month was lonely. Oh, so lonely.

This is yet another example of the purposeful repetition. Also this line is a single line below a line that also has the "oh," line in it.

Lisa awakened in the middle of the night to forceful contractions.

It feels like it has only been one month, since the marker for one month was directly stated while none others were. I think you could do well to remove any mention of time passing entirely in this segment to not set expectations for the reader.

And she didn't need the hospital.

Starting here, the next eight lines start with, or nearly start with the word "she."

one that could only be made by a hyena hyped up on crack cocaine.

This is a fun descriptor, but it breaks immersion severely. I strongly suggest finding something less comical to compare her laugh to.

'you hate me! I hate you! I hate you, Lisa!'

I could be wrong here, but shouldn't these be quotation marks?

"What?!"

Personal preference, I don't really like the combining of "?" and "!" consider just saying "'What?'"

His hair was still curly, but it was now the same bright shade of blonde as her hair. He opened his eyes and they were no longer that hideous blue, but an identical shade of brown to hers.

This is a good line, it lets readers remember the times you explicitly stated their different hair color and eye color, a good little "ohhhh" moment.

The final line is satisfying and would clear up any confusion on the part of the reader toward how the relationships between all of the people worked.

I mentioned before, the falling action after George comes crawling out feels like dropping a stone and it ends quite quickly too.

Despite all I had to say about it, I think you wrote a horrifying story with great characterization, foreshadowing, setup and all that and it was very enjoyable to read. Just watch out for all that repetition I mentioned and polish it up a bit.

his newborn mouth still full of baby teeth.

Oh my God it's a newborn talking with a full set of baby teeth, why do you have to conjure these images?

item.title: Impregnating Ultrasound
item.content:encoded:
http://kontainer.djkakt.us/impregnating-ultrasound-secondary-draft

Word count: 3800-ish

Concerns:

  • Pacing
  • Character development
  • Dialogue
  • Story
  • Dynamic between Lisa and James
  • Enough show as well as not too much tell

A woman with a bad childhood vows to have her own kid to give them what she never had. They discovers she is sterile and settles for adoption. One day, she finds an anomalous ultrasound that impregnates the woman with a de-aged version of whatever operator is using it at the time. After that, she realizes her adoptive son can truly be hers.
